title: Return to Me: The Horsemen and the Horns
summary: Zechariah's first message calls the people to return to the LORD and not to repeat the stubbornness of their fathers, who ignored the prophets until judgment overtook them. Three months later he sees the first two of eight night visions: horsemen who report that the whole earth is at rest while Jerusalem still lies in ruins, followed by God's promise to return with mercy, and four horns that scattered Judah, which four craftsmen come to throw down.
story: The exiles have been home from Babylon for nearly twenty years, but the temple is still unbuilt and the city still broken. Two months earlier Haggai had stirred the people to begin building again (Haggai 1), and the work was under way. Zechariah's opening words go beneath the building project to the heart: before anything else, return to God. Then, in the first of his visions, he hears the question the whole community is asking, how long will this go on, and God's answer, that he is jealous for Jerusalem and will return to it. The chapter sets the pattern of the book: a call to turn, a painful look at history, and promises that the story is not over.
historical:
Verse 1 dates the first message to the eighth month of the second year of Darius, October or November of 520 BC. Darius I had taken the Persian throne in 522 BC and spent his first year crushing revolts from Babylon to Media; by early 519 BC his empire was largely settled. That is the background of the riders' report in verse 11 that all the earth is at rest and tranquil. For the great powers, peace had returned. For Jerusalem, nothing had changed.

The visions are dated to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Shebat, around February 519 BC (verse 7), exactly five months after work on the temple had resumed (Haggai 1:15). The angel's lament in verse 12 speaks of God's anger with Jerusalem for seventy years. Jeremiah had spoken of seventy years of Babylonian rule (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10), and from the destruction of the temple in 587 or 586 BC to this vision was close to seventy years. The four horns stand for the powers that scattered God's people. The number four suggests the four directions, all the nations that had attacked Judah from every side, rather than four particular empires, although some interpreters have tried to name them.
cultural:
Several images in the chapter drew on the world of the Persian Empire. Persian kings were famous for their network of mounted couriers and royal agents, sometimes called the king's eyes and ears, who carried messages and reported on the provinces. Zechariah's horsemen, sent to patrol the earth and report back, picture God as the true king over the whole world, whose agents see everything. The myrtle, a fragrant evergreen shrub that grew in low, damp places, was later among the branches used for the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:15).

The horn was a common picture of strength in the ancient world, drawn from the horns of a bull or wild ox. To lift up a horn meant to exert power or pride; to cut off a horn was to break that power. The craftsmen (the Hebrew word covers workers in wood, stone, or metal) are the answer to the horns: skilled workers who can cut down what has been raised up. The measuring line of verse 16 was a builder's cord used to lay out a construction site, a sign that rebuilding is coming.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-6 are a prophetic sermon in the tradition of the earlier prophets, built on a play on the verb return: return to me, and I will return to you. It draws on history, and it ends with the fathers themselves admitting that God did what he said he would do. From verse 7 the book shifts into vision. Zechariah sees scenes that are strange and symbolic, asks what they mean, and an interpreting angel explains; this pattern of seeing, asking, and hearing will run through the next six chapters. The first vision (verses 7-17) is set at night in a hollow among myrtles and moves from the riders' report to the angel's lament to God's comforting answer. The second (verses 18-21) is short and pointed. In the Hebrew text verses 18-21 are numbered as the opening of chapter 2.

outline.t: Return to me, and I will return to you
First vision: the horsemen among the myrtles
How long? God's jealous love for Jerusalem
Second vision: four horns and four craftsmen

doctrines.note: The chapter's first command is to return to the LORD, and God attaches a promise to it: he will return to them. Repentance here is not a feeling but a turning of the whole life, and it is set against the fathers who refused to listen until it was too late.

God's riders patrol the whole earth and report to him. The empires that feel secure are watched, and their calm is no sign that God has forgotten his people. He rules the nations even when the nations appear to rule themselves.

God admits he was angry with his people, and says the nations who punished them went beyond what he intended. Judgment is real, and it has limits; those who carry it out in cruelty are themselves judged.

words.note: Shuv, to return or turn back. It is one of the most common verbs in the Old Testament and the prophets' main word for repentance. Verse 3 uses it both ways: the people are to turn to God, and God will turn back to them. Verse 16 repeats it as God's promise to return to Jerusalem with mercy.

Qanah, to be jealous or zealous. Applied to God it does not mean petty envy but the fierce, protective love of a husband for his wife or a king for his city, a love that will not share its beloved with rivals. God's jealousy for Zion is the reason he will act for her.

Qeren, horn. The word is used literally for animal horns and for the horns of the altar, and figuratively for strength and pride. The horns of verses 18-21 are nations whose power scattered Judah; the craftsmen come to break that power.

Rachamim, compassion or mercy. The word is related to the Hebrew for womb and describes a deep, tender pity. The angel asks how long God will withhold it (verse 12), and God answers that he will return to Jerusalem with it (verse 16).

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic rather than predictive. The call to return to God so that he will return to his people is the call that John the Baptist and Jesus renewed, repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near (Matthew 3:2; 4:17), and James echoes Zechariah's promise directly: draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (James 4:8). The angel of the LORD who intercedes for Jerusalem, asking God how long he will withhold mercy, pictures a mediator pleading for God's people, which Christians have seen fulfilled in Christ's intercession (Hebrews 7:25). And God's promise to return to Jerusalem, to dwell there and rebuild his house, is fulfilled in the New Testament's view when God comes to his people in the person of his Son, who calls his own body the temple (John 2:19-21).

hard.q: If God was only a little angry, why was the destruction of Jerusalem so terrible?
hard.a: Verse 15 says that God was a little angry but that the nations added to the calamity. It is a hard line to read after the horrors of the Babylonian siege. The point is not that God took Judah's sin lightly; verses 2-6 insist that his anger was great and justified. The point is that the nations used as his instruments went far beyond the judgment he intended, acting out of cruelty and ambition rather than justice. Isaiah makes a similar charge against Babylon (Isaiah 47:6) and against Assyria (Isaiah 10:5-15). Interpreters differ on how far to press the word little: some take it as relative (brief anger compared with lasting mercy, as in Isaiah 54:7-8), others as a contrast between God's measured purpose and the nations' excess. Both readings agree that God holds even the agents of his judgment responsible for their own violence.

questions: The fathers admitted God had dealt with them justly only after judgment came. What would it look like to listen before that point?
The riders report that the world is at rest while God's people are in ruins. How do you respond when the world seems settled and God seems slow?
God answers the angel with kind and comforting words. What comfort does it give you that God is jealous for his people?
